To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
liquidity risk is a significant determinant of interbank overnight rates, and that this is explained by hoarding behavior of liquidity-short banks and short-squezing behavior of liquidity-long ones.
liquidity risk, as measured by the bank's liquidity position, has a significant and robust effect on e-MID interbank rates.
liquidity-short banks pay higher rates than liquidity-long banks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pricing of liquidity risk and the behavior of liquidity-short banks in times of turmoil.
the pricing of interbank loans and the role of liquidity factors in the recent financial crisis.
the pricing of liquidity risk in a market where the liquidity risk premium is not fully explained by counterparty risk and where market imperfections are present.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the liquidity premium is the result of a combination of market imperfections, liquidity risk and counterparty risk, with the last one being the most important.
banks with higher funding and liquidity risks pay an interest rate risk premium, and that this is explained by hoarding behavior and short squeezing.
banks with higher funding risk pay a premium in the interbank market even when counterparty and market risk factors are controlled for, because they are more likely to hoard and short-squeeze.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the Euro overnight money markets, banks with high liquidity risk are punished with higher rates, but only during the turmoil periods, when the ECB did not provide enough liquidity to banks.
the e-MID market is not completely liquid, but it is still a very liquid one.
the e-MID rates are not only a function of the market's assessment of counterparty risk, but they also depend on the liquidity status of the borrower.
The main takeaway from our work is that
liquidity factors, which have received less attention in the literature, should be taken into account when assessing banks' funding liquidity risk.
banks with higher funding risk pay a premium even when other risk factors are controlled for.
the liquidity status of banks has a significant impact both before and within the turmoil periods.
